## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a07-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Shifted, not saved</dt><dd>Moving use to another hour keeps the energy; with extra energy needed it takes more.</dd>
<dt>Why it still pays</dt><dd>The moved MWh are made by cheaper, cleaner plants: spare sun instead of the peaker.</dd>
<dt>Attributed against emitted</dt><dd>Average factors can book a cut that the plants never make; marginal ones follow the plants.</dd>
<dt>A virtual power plant</dt><dd>An aggregator pools many small devices and offers their cut as one resource.</dd>
<dt>Who earns</dt><dd>Value per kW is similar; a fixed cost per device eats small devices' share.</dd>
<dt>The wires</dt><dd>Use that all comes back at once can overload a feeder, a local distribution line; a staggered restart fits.</dd>
<dt>Local trade</dt><dd>It moves money, not electricity: the kWh flow the same way either way.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Four numbers a shift report should keep apart</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A 5% flexible share in Prairie Town on 9 June 2025 (CO₂ in metric tonnes, t):

| Without losses | Cheapest | Lowest attributed CO₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Moved out | 99 MWh | 161 MWh |
| Energy saved | 0 MWh | 0 MWh |
| Running cost | −$5,995 | −$5,995 |
| Plants' CO₂ | −42.8 t | −42.8 t |
| Attributed CO₂ | −17.5 t | −22.0 t |

| With 10% extra energy | Cheapest | Lowest attributed CO₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Moved out | 90 MWh | 150 MWh |
| Energy saved | −9 MWh | −15 MWh |
| Running cost | −$5,634 | −$5,396 |
| Plants' CO₂ | −39.5 t | −37.3 t |
| Attributed CO₂ | −16.7 t | −20.8 t |

- **Moved against saved.** A shift moves MWh; only using less saves them.
- **Attributed against emitted.** Attributed CO₂ counts each MWh at its hour's [average factor]{.lx-term term="average-emission-factor"}; the plants' CO₂ is what they burn, re-dispatched.
- **Which question.** Inventories use the first; asking what a change does to the plants needs the second (case file [CF6](cf6-shifting-load-to-clean-hours.html)).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Baselines: measuring use that did not happen</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A cut is a difference.** It is what a home would have used minus what it used; the first number is never metered.
- **A [baseline]{.lx-term term="baseline"}.** Programs estimate it from similar recent days, often adjusted to the morning of the event.
- **Errors both ways.** A baseline set too high pays for cuts that never happened; one set too low misses real ones.
- **Another way.** Compare enrolled homes with a similar group that was not called (M14, upcoming).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The shift as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Take use $d_t$ in hour $t$ (MWh), flexible share $s$, extra energy $\ell$ and users' cost $u$ per MWh moved. Decide $x_t \ge 0$ (moved out) and $y_t \ge 0$ (added), with the gas plants $c_t$ and $p_t$ (MWh):

$$\min \sum_t \left(40\, c_t + 100\, p_t\right) + u \sum_t x_t$$

- **Rules.** $x_t, y_t \le s\, d_t$; $\sum_t y_t = (1 + \ell) \sum_t x_t$; each hour balances, with $0 \le c_t \le 150$ and $0 \le p_t \le 100$, and spare sun may be spilled.
- **The page's rule.** It moves use from the dearest hour to the cheapest, one straight piece of the merit order at a time. For every setting on the page it reaches this program's minimum (checked with HiGHS).
- **Ties.** Hours with the same price can trade places, so the hours moved are one choice among equally cheap ones; the cost and the plants' CO₂ are the same in all of them.
- **Next.** Carbon in models comes in M6 (upcoming); a microgrid that runs through an outage in [M5](m05-microgrid-size-and-run.html).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a07-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="saves" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Moving electricity use to another hour reduces the total electricity used.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The 5% cheapest shift moves 99 MWh and saves 0 MWh; with 10% extra energy the town uses 9 MWh more. Using less is a different response: the pool's warmer homes skip 4 MWh an event.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Moving use to hours with a lower average CO₂ factor always cuts what the plants emit.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The attributed goal moves 62 MWh more than the cheapest shift and books 4.5 t more attributed savings, yet the plants emit the same: those moves swap hours with the same plant on the margin.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="small" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every small device is worth enrolling.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At $40 a device for coordination, a thermostat's owner loses $4 a year, while a dairy still earns $11,556.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="feeder" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A virtual power plant can overload a feeder after the event is over.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Released at once, Feeder 7 carries 3.25 MW at 23:00 against its 3.0 MW rating; a staggered restart keeps it at 2.58 MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a07">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="baseline" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Air-conditioned homes are called on the month's hottest evening. Their <span class="lx-term" data-term="baseline">baseline</span>, an estimate of what they would have used, averages ten cooler, otherwise similar weekdays at the same hours. How does the measured cut compare with the real one?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Smaller</li><li data-value="b">Larger</li><li data-value="c">The same</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Smaller: in the hotter event hours the homes would have used more than on the cooler days, so the baseline is too low. Programs may adjust it for weather or for the same day's earlier use.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card a7-practice">
<!-- a07-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>Shifted or saved?</b> A program moves 10 MWh from 20:00 to 03:00, when the combined-cycle plant is on the margin. What does the town save in energy, money and CO₂?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Energy: none. Money: $600 (the peaker's $100 for the combined-cycle plant's $40, per MWh). CO₂: 1.8 t (0.55 − 0.37 t per MWh).</p></details></li><li><p><b>Extra energy.</b> With 10% extra energy needed, the 5% cheapest shift moves 90 MWh. How much more energy does the town use, and why does it still save money?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>9 MWh more (99 MWh in for 90 MWh out). Each MWh leaves a $40 or $100 hour and arrives in a $0 one, so the running cost still falls $5,634.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The thermostat's year.</b> One thermostat cuts 1.2 kW and 70% of homes take part. At $50 per kW a year for being ready, what is that part of its value?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>1.2 × 0.7 = 0.84 kW × $50 = $42. With the energy it saves, $45 a year.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Where coordination bites.</b> At what coordination cost per device does a thermostat's owner earn nothing?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>At $36 a year: 80% of its $45 value. A dairy earns $11,566 at $30.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The feeder.</b> Feeder 7 is rated 3.0 MW; released at once, its load reaches 3.25 MW at 23:00. Name two fixes.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Stagger the restart over several hours, or enrol fewer chargers on this feeder; a feeder-aware aggregator plans with the limit.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The neighbours' trade.</b> At 5¢ a kWh, 168 kWh a month change hands. Who gains and who pays?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The seller $8, the buyer $8; other customers pay the $16 of plant-and-wire charge the trade skips. The kWh and the plants do not change.</p></details></li></ol>
<!-- a07-practice:end -->
</div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>What a shift is worth depends on how it is counted.</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:ghg"><p>In the reported scenarios, reductions in <span class="lx-term" data-term="attributed-emissions">attributed emissions</span> were on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less.</p><p>Reductions are computed under average-emission-intensity accounting with perfect foresight; they are not estimates of the consequential (marginal) system response.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2025), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2025.100367">Cell Reports Sustainability</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">The full case: case file <a href="cf6-shifting-load-to-clean-hours.html">CF6</a> (how much shifting load to cleaner hours can cut emissions, and when).</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>From the course author's research: in the modeled supply chains, each open factory or warehouse could run its own <span class="lx-term" data-term="microgrid">microgrid</span>, with on-site wind, solar and storage, an energy balance every hour, and energy bought from and sold to the grid.</p><p>Because the <span class="lx-term" data-term="transactive-energy">transactive energy</span> market brought a new revenue stream, locations with stronger renewables became competitive to establish facilities despite higher fixed and logistics cost.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Holds when: stylized networks with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy. Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</p>
```
